paragraphs.text: A possessive article answers one question: whose is it? The word you choose depends on the owner, never on the thing being owned. The owner is {{de:ich}}, you write {{de:mein}}; the owner is {{de:du}}, you write {{de:dein}}; the owner is {{de:er}}, you write {{de:sein}}. One owner, one possessive — that part is as simple as English.

The second half of the job is the ending. The possessive has to agree with the noun standing behind it, the way {{de:der}}, {{de:die}} and {{de:das}} would. A masculine or neuter noun takes no ending, a feminine or plural noun takes {{de:-e}}. That is why the Dobart homepage can print {{de:Hannes und sein Motorrad}} — {{de:der Motorrad}}, so {{de:sein}} stays bare — but {{de:Lena und ihre Geige}}, because {{de:die Geige}} wants the {{de:-e}}.
mein Vater · dein Kind · sein Sohn · ihre Tochter · unser Büro · euer Hund · ihre Kinder · Ihr Termin

Two details deserve your attention. The plural of {{de:euer}} drops nothing in speech but writes {{de:eure}} as soon as the ending arrives: {{de:euer Hund}}, {{de:eure Kinder}}. And the polite {{de:Ihr}} is spelled with a capital letter, exactly like the pronoun {{de:Sie}} it belongs to — a small capital that marks the whole sentence as formal.

paragraphs.text: These are entries in the Dobart guestbook. Decide who is writing and who they are talking about: the writer gives you the person, the noun behind the gap gives you the ending.

items.sentence: Ich habe zwei Mäuse und ___ Bruder hat einen Hamster.
Lena und ___ Geige! Wie lange spielt sie schon?

paragraphs.text: Draw a pronoun card and a noun card, as exercise 10c says, and build the sentence that belongs together. The owner decides which possessive you need; the article on the noun card decides whether an ending goes on the end.
